# 🚀 Introducing Our New Sync Engine: A Paradigm Shift In Workflow

Here's the thing. When it comes to file sync, most teams have just accepted that things break.

What nobody tells you is that the breakage is almost always a queue problem, not a network problem. It's not a bandwidth issue. It's an ordering issue. The truth is, at the end of the day, everybody is solving the wrong half.

So we decided to delve into the ordering layer and leverage a robust, seamless, ever-evolving approach to streamline the whole thing. What if I told you the fix was 200 lines?

The best part: it learns. Our agent watches your folder. The assistant notices a conflict. The tool resolves it before you see a spinner. Studies show that most sync failures are actually recoverable, and industry experts agree that ordering is fundamentally the core problem.

The new engine serves as a centralized hub for conflict resolution, marking a pivotal moment for the platform and highlighting our team's commitment to innovation. It significantly improves engineering productivity. That last part matters more than it sounds.

We made a decision to rebuild rather than patch, because the old design simply has the ability to handle only one writer at a time. The decision emerged from three months of incident reports. Not a rewrite. Not a patch. A rebuild.

Honestly, the old code was a **complete disaster** and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I think it was probably my fault for shipping it in the first place, though I'd argue the deadline deserves some blame too. It was fast, simple, and reliable, right up until it wasn't. Ha.

The rollout is truly straightforward. It literally takes one command. The migration runs in order to preserve your history. Going forward, we will be shipping weekly. Let's dive in.

We cut median sync latency from 4.2 seconds to 380 milliseconds across 1,900 workspaces. That's it. That's the whole thing.

The result: It Worked.

In conclusion, the new sync engine is a multifaceted improvement that underscores our commitment to reliability. The future of sync isn't coming. It's already here.
